query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Optimized thermo-mechanical treatment of the equiatomic FCC CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) alloy enhances its inherent ductility by refining its microstructure to promote increased dislocation mobility and deformation twinning.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or cold-rolled CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) alloy exhibiting a standard FCC microstructure with moderate ductility.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermo-mechanical treatment involving an optimized cold rolling step followed by precise low-temperature annealing.
generation.conditions: Ambient conditions (room temperature and standard loading rates) typical of ductility testing.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure characterized by reduced grain size, optimized dislocation density, and balanced stacking fault energy.
generation.mechanism: The improved ductility is expected to result from enhanced activity of multiple slip systems and the promotion of deformation twinning that relieves local stress concentrations, thereby delaying crack initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in tensile elongation (ductility) without a significant loss in strength relative to conventionally processed samples.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing of the alloy that produces a typical FCC microstructure with its standard ductile behavior.
generation.boundary: The improvements may be limited if residual stresses or unexpected precipitate formation counteract the beneficial effects of the optimized processing; the precise magnitude of ductility enhancement is uncertain until experimentally verified.
generation.uncertainty: While the general trend toward increased ductility is supported by the FCC nature and prior studies on thermo-mechanical processing, the exact quantitative improvement and the interplay with strength require experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a set of CoCrFeMnNi alloy samples with identical initial conditions. Subject one group to the optimized thermo-mechanical treatment (optimized cold rolling followed by controlled low-temperature annealing) while processing a control group with conventional methods. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM for dislocation density and EBSD for grain size) on both groups.
measurements: Tensile elongation and yield strength from mechanical testing
Dislocation density and grain size measured via TEM and EBSD
Quantitative analysis of deformation twins and stacking fault features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples undergoing optimized treatment do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (i.e., tensile elongation) and the anticipated microstructural refinements (enhanced dislocation mobility and increased twin density) compared to the conventionally processed control, then the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . The requirements for designing novel metallic alloys that are capable of surpassing a whole set of specific properties of currently available commercial alloys are, at present, a subject of high demand in the industry. For instance, an improved combination of metallic alloys should possess strength and ductility while maintaining a relatively low cost. This is especially true when one is dealing with materials for high-temperature applications. Therefore, new engineering solutions are needed for novel materials that outperform the capabilities of the currently used Ni-based alloys. One of the prospective innovative materials that could be able to meet the requirements of such demanding applications, especially in the aviation and aerospace industries, may be refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). These are also known by other names, such as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). These materials have been extensively studied in recent years [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] due to their very interesting combination of properties in some of the compositions.

decision.trend: Over the past several years, researchers have increasingly turned to high‐entropy alloy systems to explore and optimize ductile behavior. Early work focused on phase composition and the role of multiphase precipitates (as in some multiphase HEAs) while later studies centered on understanding intrinsic deformation mechanisms in materials with FCC structures. For example, studies investigating the CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) alloy have examined how its face‐centered cubic structure, abundant slip systems, and adjustable stacking fault energy contribute to its room‑temperature ductility. These efforts have used a variety of processing and thermo‑mechanical approaches to tailor dislocation mobility, stacking fault energies, and microstructural features that underlie ductile performance.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, the precise tuning of the microstructural parameters that directly dictate ductility in inherently ductile FCC systems remains an open question. In particular, how controlled thermo‑mechanical processing methods can optimize dislocation slip and twinning in FCC metals—while maintaining a balance between strength and ductility—is still not fully understood.
decision.lever: controlled thermo‐mechanical treatment (e.g., optimized cold rolling followed by precise low‑temperature annealing)
decision.why: Given the inherent ductility of FCC metals such as the Cantor alloy, and following the trend of employing processing routes to finely tune microstructural features (grain size, dislocation density, and stacking fault energy), an optimized thermo‑mechanical treatment is the most plausible next step. This approach builds on the established success of processing strategies to adjust deformation mechanisms and is directly targeted at enhancing ductility under ambient conditions.
